source_read: Accepted manuscript PDF, 10 pages (text PDF pp. 1-5, references pp. 5-7, Table 1 pp. 8-10), all pages read; text pages checked on renders at 150 dpi, Table 1 (PDF pp. 8-10) at 300 dpi, reference list PDF p. 6 rendered; cited as PDF p. N (pagination differs from the version of record). Step 1 written before the card was opened; Petrie 1996 read blind in the same session.

claims.overstatement: No material overstatement of this source; minor points. (1) 'During 57 days when morphine solution was their only fluid': Table 1 (PDF p. 8) says the 57-day forced period included 4 choice days, so morphine was not the only fluid on those days; add 'apart from 4 choice days'. (2) 'these animal studies cannot show anything about people' is firmer than the review, which calls Rat Park's value as a model of human addictive behaviour questionable (PDF p. 5) and the popular reading overstated (PDF p. 4); the claim's closing sentence ('not shown by these designs') matches the review and is the safer wording. (3) The 1981 housing difference was broadly driven by males, with less evidence in females (Table 1, PDF p. 9); the claim does not say so. (4) The Nichols-cycle F = 200.9 carries df 1/69 although at most 28 rats remained, so it cannot be a between-rat test; the review does not say how it was built, so it should not be read as a measure of effect size.
claims.note: Every number the claim takes from this source was re-found on the rendered pages: 18.6 vs 13.3 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat in the 57-day forced period, F = 200.9 (df 1/69) for Nichols-cycle choice days and F 26.38 (df 1/23) for the abstinence choice days (Table 1, PDF p. 8); 1979 housing effect only with 10% sucrose, largest at 0.15 mg/ml (PDF p. 9); 1981 F = 33.64, p < 0.0001, no df printed (PDF p. 9). Group sizes by housing condition are 10 and 22 (1978), 18 and 18 (1979) and 8 per group (1981), which gives the claim's '8 to 22'. 'No account of pregnancies' paraphrases the review's statement that the papers do not say how offspring of the mixed-sex colony were dealt with (PDF p. 3). The review describes Petrie (1996) as a replication of the 1979 study (PDF p. 4), but Petrie states his work was designed to replicate the 1981 study (Petrie p. 398); the claim correctly names 1981 and cites Petrie for it. The review's other replication paragraph (Hill & Powell; Bozarth et al., dated 1987 in the text and 1989 in the reference list) matches the claim's 'point both ways' sentence.

anchors.extracted: Rat Park = a series of studies from the late 1970s led by Bruce Alexander at Simon Fraser University, Vancouver; socially housed rats were less likely to drink oral morphine than isolated rats; the work is cited in popular talks, a comic and by drug-policy campaigners; the summary says the authors' measured conclusions have been lost in translation.

Enclosure: L-shaped, 8.8 m2, cedarwood sawdust, open boxes, tubes, open-topped cages and a climbing pole. 32 albino Wistar rats: 4 females and 6 males alone in 18 x 25 x 18 cm cages without sight of neighbours; 10 females and 12 males in Rat Park. For 3 weeks beforehand all had water and morphine hydrochloride solution and drank almost only water.

Measurement differed by housing: isolated rats' bottles weighed and corrected against a bottle on an empty cage for leakage and evaporation; Rat Park rats drank from a one-rat tube where single drops were released, counted and filmed with the rat's identifying mark.

Three intake measures, eight forced-choice days, four groups (housing x sex). After what the text calls four deaths, 2 isolated females, 6 isolated males, 7 colony females and 12 colony males remained (27 of 32, i.e. five fewer). Groups very small; isolated females (2 rats) drank most in all periods; broadly isolated > Rat Park and females > males; over the four choice days of the 3-day cycle isolated intake rose and Rat Park intake fell; Rat Park rats did drink morphine, contrary to some reports.
The original authors' conclusions were measured: sex and housing are important variables, and theories that ignore them risk oversimplification.

1979 study: morphine-naive rats chose between tap water and a morphine solution made more palatable (sweeter, weaker) in 5-day steps; isolated rats drank more than Rat Park rats, and females more than males, only at high sweetness and low morphine concentration.
1981 study: rats raised in Rat Park or isolation, half switched at 65 days; rats in Rat Park drank less morphine whatever their rearing; no sex differences.

Limitations: different data collection for colony and isolated rats allows systematic bias (e.g. leakage underestimated only in cages), partly offset because water intake did not show the same pattern; males and females lived together and the papers do not say how offspring were handled (pregnancy and weaning could bias intake); colony competition; small samples and complex designs allow many analyses and raise false-positive risk.

The original papers nowhere link the findings to human addiction or to deprivation; only after ending the animal work did Alexander use Rat Park for an adaptive model of drug use (lectures, writings, a popular book).

anchors.locator: Replication attempts and contemporaneous studies, 1st paragraph (refs. 12 and 25 on PDF p. 6)
anchors.extracted: Independent attempts gave mixed results. Hill & Powell (ref. 12, 1976): Wistar rats reared enriched or impoverished did not differ in morphine intake; enriched rats drank more cocaine-containing water. A study the text dates 1987 (ref. 25, Bozarth, Murray & Wise, 1989, title covering heroin and cocaine): isolated rats quickly learned to lever-press for intravenous cocaine, socially housed rats did not consistently.

anchors.locator: Replication attempts and contemporaneous studies, 1st paragraph (Petrie sentences)
anchors.extracted: Petrie (1996) is described as replicating the 1979 study (ref. 17) with two recording methods meant to remove the measurement bias; colony intake was broadly similar to Rat Park's, isolated rats drank substantially less than Rat Park's isolated rats; Petrie points to a change in the Wistar stock (possible genetic cause). Petrie himself names the 1981 study (Petrie p. 398).

Rat Park models one manipulation (housing) on one behaviour (morphine self-administration), so the popular reading that it gave a new understanding of addiction is overstated; supply, availability and opportunity are proximal determinants of human use; in human research 'environment' also covers access to services and social exclusion.

Group differences emerged only in very specific conditions (rats pre-exposed to morphine, precise morphine and sucrose concentrations, certain stages); group sizes extremely small; many comparisons per study.

Whether Rat Park is an accurate model of human addictive behaviour is called questionable; most rodent self-administration studies still house animals singly; human drug use and problem use arise from interacting individual and social factors, not social environment alone.

anchors.locator: Table 1, 1978 study row (Number of rats, Key manipulations, Main findings)
anchors.extracted: Isolated 4 F + 6 M, enriched 10 F + 12 M. Limited-access data not presented (measurement error). Forced period: morphine HCl only for 57 days with 4 choice days; mean intake enriched 18.6 vs isolated 13.3 mg morphine HCl per rat (no time base); two females per group died. Nichols cycles (8 three-day cycles, 4 choice days): isolated drank less on all but choice days, more on choice days, F = 200.9, df 1/69, p < 0.001. Abstinence (choice days after 2 and 5 weeks): isolated more, F 26.38, df 1/23, p < 0.001; one enriched female died.

9 F + 9 M per housing; 5 days per solution (0.5 mg/ml with 0-10% sucrose, then 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose); little housing effect at high morphine/low sucrose; with 10% sucrose isolated rats drank more, largest difference at 0.15 mg/ml + 10% sucrose; sex differences inconsistent.

Four groups of 4 F + 4 M (isolated only, enriched only, switched either way at 65 days); 5 days per solution (10% sucrose, 0.06 mg/ml quinine, then 1, 0.5, 0.3, 0.15 mg/ml morphine HCl in 10% sucrose). Enriched at testing drank less regardless of early housing, F = 33.64, p < 0.0001 (no df); no early-housing effect; weak interaction; housing differences broadly driven by males, less evidence in females.

key_findings.correction: Table 1 (PDF p. 8) gives the forced-access period as 57 days of morphine HCl only 'with 4 choice days throughout', so 'morphine solution the only fluid for 57 days' should read 'the only fluid for 57 days apart from 4 choice days'. All statistics (18.6 vs 13.3 mg per rat; F = 200.9 df 1/69; F 26.38 df 1/23; F 7.26, 67.86, 36.44) confirmed. The abstinence result refers to the choice days after 2 and 5 weeks.

reporting_issues.note: Counts 32 -> 27 and Table 1 (2 + 2 + 1) give five deaths; text says four.

Petrie p. 398 (General Discussion, 4th paragraph) names the 1981 study; Petrie's procedure is close to, not identical with, the 1981 design in this Table 1 (4-day phases, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml, 0.05 mg/ml quinine against 5-day phases, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml, 0.06 mg/ml).
Ref. 25 on PDF p. 6: Bozarth, Murray & Wise, Pharmacol Biochem Behav 1989;33(4):903-7.
'Robbins' on PDF p. 1, 'LHCl' and the df-less F on PDF p. 9 seen on the renders.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; worst domain high (no search or criteria), so overall high is required and fits.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the summary paragraph overgeneralizes, the body and table qualify it.

missed: Table 1 prints df 1/69 for the Nichols-cycle housing and sex tests (F = 200.9 and 67.86) although at most 28 rats remained (df 1/23 elsewhere fits 27 rats in a 2 x 2 design); the error term therefore cannot be between rats, and the review does not say how the test was built (perhaps repeated days pooled). Cite the direction, not the size of F, as evidence of a housing effect.
Table 1's 1978 amounts (18.6 vs 13.3 mg morphine HCl per rat) carry no time base (per day or per period) and no body-weight correction; cite them 'as tabulated'.
